<explanation>
Below is a detailed explanation tailored for designing a system architecture diagram for Kubo (the IPFS implementation in Go). Since Kubo is a full‐featured, highly modular, peer-to-peer network node, your diagram should capture its multiple layers and subsystems. Here’s how to proceed:

1. Identify the project type and key purpose:
   • Kubo is a complete implementation of IPFS written in Go. It functions as a network node that implements content addressing, distributed file storage, peer-to-peer networking (via libp2p and the DHT), and provides both a CLI and an HTTP/RPC API for interacting with the node.
   • The project is not just a simple library—it is a full-stack network service that integrates networking, API gateways, command handling, and storage subsystems.

2. Analyze the file structure to find main modules/components:
   • CLI and Entry Points: 
     - The “cmd” directory (e.g., cmd/ipfs) contains the main entry point for starting the daemon and the CLI.
   • Core Functionality:
     - The “core” directory (with subfolders like core/commands, core/coreapi, core/corehttp, and core/node) embodies the primary business logic. This includes:
       • Command parsing and execution.
       • API implementations such as the core API and HTTP gateway.
       • Network protocols and interfaces interacting with libp2p.
   • Configuration and Initialization:
     - The “config” and “repo” directories manage system-wide settings, datastore configuration, and repository management.
   • Networking and Peer Communication:
     - Directories like “p2p”, “core/node/libp2p”, and “routing” indicate networking layers including DHT, peer discovery, and routing protocols.
   • Plugin Architecture:
     - The “plugin” directory evidences a modular and extensible design, enabling support for additional functionality (such as alternative datastore implementations).
   • Additional Functionality:
     - Components related to UnixFS (“client/rpc/unixfs.go”, “core/coreiface/unixfs.go”), block handling (“blocks”), and mounting via Fuse (“fuse”) also exist.
   • Testing and Integration:
     - The “test” directory (with subfolders for unit, integration, and sharness tests) shows the emphasis on designing for reliability and verifying interactions between modules.

3. Map out the high-level system components:
   a. Frontend Components:
      • Command-Line Interface (CLI) that initiates commands and interacts with the HTTP API.
      • WebUI (although maintained separately, it interfaces with the node via the API).
   b. Backend/Daemon Components:
      • IPFS Daemon: The running node that supports both command execution and background tasks.
      • Core API Server: Implements the HTTP RPC API (located in core/corehttp) for remote procedure calls (e.g., to add files, query the network, etc.).
   c. Networking & P2P Stack:
      • libp2p-based networking layer handling DHT, peer discovery, and data routing.
      • Bitswap engine for data trading between peers.
   d. Data Storage & Repository Management:
      • The datastore and file repository managed under “repo” that store the content-addressable files.
   e. Plugins and Extensibility:
      • The plugin system which allows alternative backend storage or custom protocols.
   f. Auxiliary Services:
      • Gateway HTTP server endpoints (for the /ipfs and /ipns routes).
      • Diagnostic, logging, and monitoring (e.g., metrics in core/corehttp/metrics.go).

4. Determine how these components interact:
   • The CLI sends commands to the daemon either directly or via the HTTP/RPC API.
   • The daemon routes the command to core modules, which in turn interact with the underlying storage (repo), network (libp2p stack), and other subsystems.
   • For web requests, the HTTP gateway accepts external requests, validates them, and translates them into internal core API calls.
   • Plugins hook into these pathways to extend capabilities (e.g., to support new datastore types).

5. Emphasize architectural design patterns:
   • Layered Architecture: Separate presentation (CLI/API), business logic (core modules), and data storage (repo) layers.
   • Modular Design: Each subsystem (networking, storage, command processing) exists in its own module or package.
   • Plug-in extensibility: Use of dynamic loading to support various plugins.
   • Clear separation between client-side logic (e.g., in “client/rpc”) and daemon/server-side code.
   
6. Guidelines for the diagram creation:
   • Use clearly labeled boxes for each high-level component: CLI, HTTP API, Daemon/Node, Libp2p/Networking, Storage/Repository, Plugins.
   • Use directional arrows to indicate the flow of commands, data, and responses between these components (for example, arrows from CLI → HTTP API → Core modules → Networking/Data Storage).
   • Consider color coding: different colors can distinguish between external interfaces (e.g., CLI, HTTP Gateway) and internal processing layers (core, networking, repository).
   • Use shapes (e.g., rectangles for services, cylinders for databases, rounded boxes for plug-ins) to help visually differentiate components.
   • Provide annotations or labels that briefly note the main technologies or responsibilities. For instance: “libp2p (Networking, DHT, Bitswap)”, “core/http (HTTP Gateway, RPC Server)”, “repo (Content-addressable datastore)”, and “plugin (Extensibility modules)”.

7. Tailoring the diagram for a full-stack network node:
   • Clearly separate frontend (CLI and WebUI integration points) and backend (daemon, API server, networking services) components.
   • Highlight internal data flows, such as command execution, peer-to-peer message exchanges, and storage operations.
   • Make sure to include design elements that illustrate real-time operations like content addressing and the interplay between the ephemeral state of the node and persistent state in the repository.

8. Final Instruction:
   In your diagram, start by listing all external interfaces (CLI, HTTP Gateway) and then layer the system internals—identify the “daemon” as the central orchestrator, show its connections to the networking modules (libp2p, DHT, Bitswap), the data repository, and the plugin layer. Use directional arrows to denote both control and data flows. A detailed diagram like this not only maps out major components but also shows the essential communication pathways that facilitate IPFS’s operation.

Following these steps and guidelines will ensure that your system design diagram accurately represents the complex and modular architecture of Kubo, providing clarity to both developers and stakeholders.
</explanation>
